NIDDK identifies diabetes as a common cause of CKD in adults and describes kidney filter damage from elevated blood glucose.

NIDDK defines diabetic kidney disease as kidney disease caused by diabetes. It explains that high glucose can damage renal blood vessels and impair their function, while kidney damage can reduce filtration of blood and allow waste to accumulate. Together these passages support renal vascular injury as a contributor to diabetic kidney dysfunction.

NIDDK states that hypertension can damage renal blood vessels and other components of the kidney filtering system. Damage to these structures can impair the kidneys' ability to remove waste and excess fluid. The page identifies high blood pressure as a common cause of chronic kidney disease.

selected_evidence.text: NIDDK states that type 2 diabetes develops when the body has difficulty using insulin and the pancreas does not make enough insulin to maintain glucose balance. Insulin resistance contributes to hyperglycemia and type 2 diabetes in the context of inadequate insulin secretion.
NIDDK includes family history in its list of type 2 diabetes risk factors.
NIDDK lists limited physical activity among reported risk factors for type 2 diabetes.
NIDDK lists overweight or obesity among circumstances associated with higher likelihood of developing type 2 diabetes.

Endotext describes insulin resistance in liver and muscle as an important pathogenic feature of type 2 diabetes; compensatory beta-cell secretion can initially maintain normal glucose, whereas inadequate beta-cell compensation permits hyperglycemia and progression to overt diabetes.

selected_evidence.text: NHLBI identifies chronic damage or weakening of heart muscle as a major cause of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Reduced ventricular contractile capacity can impair cardiac pumping and lead to heart failure. The relationship is a supported causal pathway particularly for HFrEF and does not imply that all heart failure develops through the same mechanism.
